article.content: Leading restaurateur says Gulf countries actively help businesses set up, while east Asia has a better work ethic Some of London’s top restaurants are opening branches in Dubai because of a “tax tsunami” in the UK and better work ethic abroad, according to a leading restaurateur. James Robson, a co-owner of Fallow in St James’s Market, regarded as the capital’s hottest restaurant, serving 1,000 people a day, has just signed a deal to open an outpost in the Gulf. Continue reading...
article.aiArticle:
A growing contingent of prominent London restaurateurs is bypassing the British capital in favor of expansions in the Gulf, driven by what industry figures describe as an oppressive domestic financial climate. According to **Business | The Guardian**, a leading culinary entrepreneur points to a mounting domestic **"tax tsunami"** as a primary catalyst pushing dining establishments to look outward for growth. Rather than navigating tightening margins and rising operational burdens at home, elite operators are increasingly drawn to international hubs where governments actively facilitate new commercial ventures.

## The Pull of the Gulf and East Asia

The report states that Gulf nations are aggressively courting high-end hospitality brands by providing active assistance during the setup process. Beyond favorable tax structures, industry leaders cited distinct regional advantages when expanding operations abroad. Specifically, the publication notes that East Asian markets offer a stronger and more reliable work ethic among staff compared to current domestic conditions. 

This overseas migration highlights a broader strain on domestic businesses, who often find themselves struggling with inflation and supply chain pressures—challenges that have recently forced many households to rethink spending, much like how citizens deal with wider economic anxiety by purchasing essentials such as [tinned food, loo roll and power banks](https://new-sfeed.lovable.app/en/articles/tinned-food-loo-roll-and-power-banks-the-brits-following-advice-to) based on official preparedness advice. 

## The Stakes for London’s Dining Scene

As top-tier culinary talent redirects investment toward Dubai and other international markets, the traditional dominance of London's gastronomy sector faces a serious challenge. High-profile departures risk draining local talent, reducing tax revenues for municipal authorities, and diminishing the global reputation that once made the UK capital an unchallenged destination for fine dining. For local workers and suppliers, the exodus of major hospitality groups could mean fewer high-paying creative roles and a stagnant domestic market.

## What to Watch

Observers should monitor whether mid-tier and independent restaurants follow the lead of elite operators by moving operations overseas, or if upcoming national budgets will introduce targeted relief to stem the outflow. Additionally, industry analysts will be watching to see how Gulf destinations manage the influx of foreign culinary brands over the coming fiscal quarters.

Sources: [Business | The Guardian](https://www.theguardian.com/food/2026/oct/24/uk-tsunami-taxes-top-london-restaurants-expand-abroad)
